column1: 34-009 · Don’t take painkillers for more than 15 days a month; limit combination painkillers to 10 days. Otherwise, headaches may actually be caused by the medication itself.
column2:
### 9. Don’t take painkillers for more than 15 days a month; limit combination painkillers to 10 days. Otherwise, headaches may actually be caused by the medication itself.
<!-- Cost Tag: Money=0 Time=Low Willpower=Some Benefit=Med Metric=Mortality -->
- Cost: No direct cost. You’ll just need to keep track of how many days you’ve taken the medicine, and resist the urge to pop pills at every sign of a headache.
- In plain terms: If you take painkillers frequently for recurrent headaches, the medication itself may eventually provoke more frequent headaches — a clinical condition known as medication-overuse headache. The clinical threshold is taking standard single-ingredient analgesics (such as acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or aspirin) for 15 or more days per month for at least three consecutive months. For combination analgesics containing multiple active ingredients or caffeine, the threshold drops to 10 or more days per month. Rotating between different painkillers does not reset this counter. Most patients experience substantial symptom relief after systematically tapering excess pain medication under medical guidance.
- Benefit: The third edition of the International Classification of Headache published by the International Headache Society outlines the diagnostic criteria for this condition. It applies to people who already have a history of headaches, experience headaches on 15 or more days each month, and have been regularly taking excessive amounts of headache medication for over 3 months. For standard non-opioid painkillers, the threshold for overuse is 15 days per month; for combination painkillers, it is 10 days per month. This classification is backed by robust epidemiological evidence, and most patients see positive results after reducing their medication intake.
- Evidence grade: B
- Sources: Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society (2018). The International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition. Cephalalgia, 38(1):1-211. <https://doi.org/10.1177/0333102417738202>; ICHD-3 Online Edition 8.2 Medication-overuse headache (including 8.2.3, 8.2.5). <https://ichd-3.org/8-headache-attributed-to-a-substance-or-its-withdrawal/8-2-medication-overuse-headache-moh/>
- Notes: Painkillers with “caffeine” in their name typically contain added caffeine, so they count toward the 10-day limit for combination painkillers. If you find that your headache days are increasing month on month, it’s best to consult a neurologist rather than simply taking more medication. This evidence grade is assigned because the classification criteria serve as a diagnostic benchmark rather than being derived from controlled clinical trials. The benefit level is rated “moderate” as it primarily reduces the frequency of headaches without preventing life-threatening outcomes.

column1: 34-010 · Clear out expired and unused medicines regularly; dispose of them with packaging in hazardous-waste bins, not at home

### 10. Clear out expired and unused medicines regularly; dispose of them with packaging in hazardous-waste bins, not at home
<!-- Cost Tag: Money=0 Time=Low Willpower=No Benefit=Low Metric=Mortality -->
- Cost: No cost. Sort the medicine cabinet once a year — about ten minutes.
- In plain terms: Nearly half of unsupervised pediatric medication ingestions involve prescription tablets. About three in ten of those prescriptions belong to grandparents. Removing unused drugs removes one thing a child can find. Put discarded medicines in hazardous-waste bins with original packaging, or hand them to pharmacies that collect old drugs.
- Benefit: U.S. emergency-department surveillance estimated that from 2004 to 2013, children under 6 took medicines without adult supervision about 640,000 times (estimate 640,161 ED visits). In 2013 alone about 59,000 visits (59,092). From 2010 to 2013 the most common form was oral prescription tablets, 45.9% of cases. Among prescriptions, opioids (13.8%) and benzodiazepines (12.7%) were most common. In 2017 five U.S. poison centers surveyed callers: for prescription ingestions, 30.7% involved grandparents’ medicines. More than half (51.5%) of prescription drugs had been removed from original packaging before the child accessed them. China’s National Catalogue of Hazardous Wastes (2025 edition) classifies household discarded medicines and their packaging as hazardous waste in domestic refuse. Shanghai’s sorting guide puts waste medicines in hazardous waste, including expired drugs, capsules, tablets, and inner packaging — “discard medicines preferably with packaging.” Shanghai also requires pharmacies collecting household expired medicines to use temporary transfer points set by district market-supervision departments. The U.S. FDA states the best disposal for expired and unwanted medicines is take-back programs.
- Evidence grade: B
- Sources:Lovegrove MC, Weidle NJ, Budnitz DS (2015). Trends in Emergency Department Visits for Unsupervised Pediatric Medication Exposures, 2004-2013. Pediatrics, 136(4):e821-e829. <https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2015-2092>; Agarwal M, Lovegrove MC, Geller RJ, et al. (2020). Circumstances Involved in Unsupervised Solid Dose Medication Exposures among Young Children. Journal of Pediatrics, 219:188-195.e6. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpeds.2019.12.027>; et al. (2024). column1: 34-011 · While taking cephalosporins, metronidazole, and similar antibacterials, and for 7 days after stopping, avoid alcohol — including alcohol in Huoxiang Zhengqi oral liquid and cough syrups
column2:
### 11. While taking cephalosporins, metronidazole, and similar antibacterials, and for 7 days after stopping, avoid alcohol — including alcohol in Huoxiang Zhengqi oral liquid and cough syrups
<!-- Cost Tag: Money=0 Time=Low Willpower=Some Benefit=Low Metric=Mortality -->
- Cost: No money. Abstain from alcohol for a little over a week; check other medicines for ethanol on the label.
- In plain terms: Some cephalosporins and metronidazole can trigger flushing, palpitations, chest tightness, and vomiting when mixed with alcohol; severe cases drop blood pressure. Beer and spirits are not the only triggers — Huoxiang Zhengqi oral liquid and cough syrups with alcohol count. Avoid alcohol from the start of the drug through 7 days after the last dose.
- Benefit: This is a disulfiram-like reaction. A 2023 medication-safety popularization from the Fujian Provincial Medical Products Administration states that drinking before or after some cephalosporins may trigger this reaction, “which can seriously harm health or be life-threatening.” Symptoms include facial flushing, sweating, palpitations, even dyspnea, hypotension, and anaphylactic shock. Citing the Chinese Pharmacopoeia Clinical Medication Information, listed drugs include cefazolin, ceftriaxone, cefoperazone, metronidazole, tinidazole, furazolidone, and others. The article states “no alcohol or alcohol-containing drugs or foods for 7 days after dosing,” examples including liqueur chocolates and Huoxiang Zhengqi oral liquid, because the inhibited enzyme often needs 4 to 5 days to recover. One Guangzhou hospital summarized 82 cases over 2 years: cephalosporins caused 57 cases (69.51%), nitroimidazoles (metronidazole, tinidazole) 10 cases (12.20%). Alcohol from beverages 40 cases (48.78%), from ethanol-containing medicines 31 cases (37.80%) — including Huoxiang Zhengqi oral liquid, cough syrup, and motherwort extract. Of 82 cases, 68 mild, 9 moderate, 5 severe; relief within 1–3 hours; no deaths. U.S. metronidazole labeling requires no alcohol during treatment and for at least 3 days after, and no products containing propylene glycol.
- Evidence grade: B
- Sources: Fujian Provincial Food and Drug Administration (Fujian Provincial Drug Science Popularization and Supervision Data Center) (2023). Analysis of 82 cases of disulfiram-like reactions in our hospital. Chinese Pharmacy, 26(29):4089-4091. <https://doi.org/10.6039/j.issn.1001-0408.2015.29.19>; Pfizer (2026). Tell the doctor if you drank recently when these are prescribed. The popularization also suggests avoiding alcohol for 3 days before dosing while noting no authoritative interval. If flushing or palpitations start, stop all alcohol immediately; mild cases may resolve on their own, severe cases need hospital care. Do not drink alcohol while taking acetaminophen — item 1 in this section. Rated B because evidence is case series and labeling, not controlled trials. Benefit rated small: all 82 cases recovered within hours, no deaths, only 5 severe.
